summary:
Private sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex is legal in the Central African Republic for both men and women. Criminal liability attaches only to conduct in public.

Article 85 of the criminal code punishes public expression of love between persons of the same sex as an attack on public morals. The penalty is six months to two years' imprisonment or a fine of 150,000 to 600,000 CFA francs ($300 to $1,200), a heavier sanction than the code applies to other public-morals offences. Where one participant is a child, the adult faces two to five years' imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs ($200 to $1,600).

The US State Department's 2012 human rights report recorded no arrests or detentions by police under these provisions. Alternatives Centrafrique, a domestic organisation, has since documented arrests prompted by false accusations of same-sex intercourse, as well as mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement. The 2023 State Department report recorded no reports of violence against LGBTQ people, which leaves open whether incidents were absent or went unreported.

Criminalisation of public same-sex affection, together with cultural stigma, keeps the LGBTQ community concealed. The 2023 State Department report found no known organisations promoting LGBTQ human rights. Issues of sexual orientation and gender identity are treated as taboo and described publicly as imported from Europe and contrary to African values.

Legal gender recognition does not exist in the Central African Republic. A trans visitor cannot obtain a changed gender marker and will be assessed by officials against documents as issued. Sources provide no transgender-specific criminal, documentary, screening, facilities, custody or care rule beyond that absence; the remaining rules are stated only on an LGBTQ-collective or homosexuality-specific basis, and no transgender-specific statement on societal tolerance is documented.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in health, employment, education, or access to goods and services. Marriage is defined in Article 7 of the constitution as the union between one man and one woman, and no same-sex couple can be legally recognised. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and family and marriage are placed under the protection of the state.

No law bars psychological or medical practices used as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data treats sexual orientation as sensitive data, and Article 17 prohibits any processing of sensitive data on the ground that it risks discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms. The provision names sexual orientation; gender identity is not addressed.

The Central African Republic signed the United Nations joint statement condemning violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. It has received two Universal Periodic Review recommendations, on non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and on improving the situation of sexual minorities. The OHCHR summary of stakeholder submissions for the country's fourth-cycle review, examined at the 45th session in January 2024, includes related stakeholder recommendations.

Societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people is entrenched, and many citizens attribute homosexuality to undue Western influence. Discrimination in education, healthcare and employment is documented, and LGBTQ people conceal their identities to avoid it. Maintaining a relationship is described as dangerous.
tangentialFactors:
The 2012 US State Department report for the Central African Republic documents extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and by Seleka rebels, and harsh prison conditions, but contains little LGBT-specific material. No source in this inventory reports how trans detainees are held or treated in custody; the record of impunity for state violence is the only available context for anyone taken into detention.

No ban exists on surgeries intended to normalise the bodies of intersex infants, and no reports of such operations were recorded in 2023. That gap concerns intersex children rather than trans visitors, and sits alongside the absence of legal gender recognition.
localsOnly:
Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military.

A positive HIV diagnosis is used to stigmatise workers, leading to harassment, blackmail and dismissal. Religious preaching of conversion is rarely carried into practice, since LGBTQ people keep their identities hidden.

No known organisations promote LGBTQ human rights. Alternatives Centrafrique, founded in 2009 and registered in 2020, has submitted reports to the Universal Periodic Review in its third and fourth cycles.
outOfScopeNotes:
The only enforcement figure for Article 85 in this inventory dates from 2012, when no arrests or detentions were recorded; no current arrest data is sourced.

The 2023 State Department report recorded no reports of violence against LGBTQ people and could not establish whether that reflected an absence of incidents or victims not reporting. No violence data specific to transgender people in the Central African Republic is available in these sources.

No source treats gender identity separately from sexual orientation except to record the absence of a gender-recognition procedure; whether Article 17 of Law 24-001 extends to gender identity is unresolved.

No custody, screening or facilities data specific to trans travellers is sourced, and whether the absence of transgender-specific tolerance reporting reflects absent hostility or absent reporting is unresolved.
